title: The Most Valuable Step in Writing with AI Isn't the Prompt—It's Turning Editing Feedback into Compound Interest
dek: Katie takes AI from career coach to writing plugin: first load the model with context, then feed every edit back into the system to compound. For her, AI's value isn't just efficiency—it's a support system that steadies her emotions and gets her past execution hurdles.
why: Not another prompt demo, but a rare look at how one writer built her own AI workflow: how to set up context files, choose reviewers, and avoid pitfalls even as a non-technical user—all concrete and copyable.
who: Journalists and editors producing content, newsletters, or long-form pieces, plus independent developers building AI as a personal productivity system; especially those stuck with homogeneous AI output and wanting to build their own workflow.

points.h: Hiring AI as a coach is about being challenged, not being replaced
points.body: After being laid off from an editing and ghostwriting role at a crypto company, Katie tried agency, client-side, and freelance work, yet still felt her own ideas had hit a ceiling. Real career coaches were too expensive—she estimated around $150/hour—so she switched to ChatGPT at $20/month. She didn't ask it to think for her; instead, she used it as an externalized thinking partner: she'd lay out her situation, let it question and push back, especially pulling her out of herself when she tended to catastrophize. She later called this a 'thinking tool.' She even used it to decide whether to accept Every's column offer—ChatGPT advised her to try it, and she's been there ever since.

points.h: Delivering across five channels relies on context, not typing speed
points.body: In early 2025, as a freelancer, Katie severely overcommitted: within a two-week deadline she had to deliver 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts, and 16 Instagram posts. She managed not by writing faster but by what she later realized is called context engineering: first writing out the company's brand messaging, product details, audience, and differentiators, then letting the model generate. Building that context upfront was laborious, but once the foundation was set, production speed became very fast. She admits she repeated the overcommitment six months later—the method didn't cure her overcommitting habit.

points.h: Without foundational information, style constraints spin in neutral
points.body: On what should go into a project first, Katie is clear: not 'use these words, avoid those' or 'keep reading level low,' but first give the model a base profile of who the reader is, what their pain points are, how the product addresses them, and who the competitors and differentiators are. She says this is her instinct from writing style guides in content marketing, just now fed to AI. Only after the foundational material is in place do constraints on tone, wording, and syntax follow. Her take on 'style': wording issues will nag forever, but without underlying information, style constraints are just spinning in neutral.

points.h: The model is the kitchen; fresh ingredients must be brought in by humans
points.body: The 'data' she means isn't generic background but first-hand material that postdates the model's knowledge cutoff or exists only in the physical world: the company's own research, third-party reports, specific personal experiences. If you just ask the model to write a 'style guide' from what it already knows, you get commoditized information. So she sees the human's job as the 'last mile': bringing new material the model doesn't have into the system. Her metaphor: the model is the kitchen, the process is chopping and cooking, but fresh ingredients must be carried in by a person—the quality and freshness of inputs ultimately determine whether a piece is worth reading.

points.h: AI as supportive technology is as powerful as when it's a production tool
points.body: Katie shared something she rarely says publicly: she has bipolar disorder, with high-energy periods and very long lows. For her, AI's value isn't just 'high output' but lowering the friction of daily life, making it easier to function as a normal person. She'd put off booking a family doctor for three years, then had Codex automatically find nearby doctors who accepted her insurance and new patients, and make the appointment. Her inbox is also pre-filtered by automation to surface only emails that truly need her reply, rather than her digging through subscription notifications for 'bombs' every day. Her own phrasing: AI as supportive technology is as powerful as AI as productive technology.

points.h: A career coach isn't a single prompt—it's a project
points.body: That simple 'help me be a career coach' prompt has since grown into a standalone project in Codex: it contains her own profile and role positioning, Every's brand positioning intel, article performance data exported from the CMS, a validation folder collecting reader praise, and Q2/Q3 OKRs. Much of that material wasn't manually compiled: she learned from Alex Duffy to have AI interview her, drawing out her thoughts and organizing them into documents. She now increasingly talks to it aloud in 'self-talk' mode, having it prioritize, manage projects, and maintain a kanban board. She's even forgotten what's on the board, only asking when she needs a deliverable's deadline.

points.h: Writing should be like engineering: fix each issue only once
points.body: Compound Writing started as a fork of Kieran's Compound Engineering: in engineering, a system should remember every piece of feedback, fix the same issue only once, and automatically do it right next time; writing should work the same way. She mapped the engineering phases—brainstorming, planning, working, reviewing—onto writing's brainstorming, outlining, drafting, and reviewing, and designed three types of review: substantive edit for overall structure and argument, line edit for sentence-level polish, and a final publication-ready check. She no longer opens web chat windows; instead she runs this system on Claude or ChatGPT's desktop apps, with style guides, sample articles, and other context loaded in, and the human only needs to bring in fresh information. The plugin was already downloadable from Every's GitHub at the time of recording.

points.h: This plugin is a gym, not a ghostwriter
points.body: She calls the plugin a gym—its goal is to make the user stronger, not to have AI write for them. She breaks down favorite authors into invocable reviewer skills: Vonnegut says 'start as close to the end as possible, every sentence must earn its place, give the reader a character to root for'; Hitchcock talks about the 'bomb under the table'—if you let the audience see the countdown, a one-second shock becomes five minutes of suspense. She builds these frameworks directly into the editing steps, so after writing you can invoke Vonnegut, Hitchcock, Sorkin, or Sedaris to review your draft. She thinks non-professional writers might benefit even more, because they don't have the baggage of 'how I used to write better' standing in the way.

terms.def: An approach where AI remembers every piece of feedback, so each correction is given only once and applied automatically thereafter, making output continuously better.
A plugin that transplants compound engineering to the writing process, accumulating feedback on style, structure, and editing.
The practice of loading background information—brand, audience, competitors—into the system before asking the model to write, setting boundaries for the AI.
AI that doesn't produce content but reduces friction in life and execution, making it easier for a person to get things done.
Model Context Protocol, a common interface standard connecting models to external data and applications; Katie uses it to link small apps with her tools.

quotes.text: Clarity, it turns out, doesn't arrive gift wrapped from a digital assistant or even a human coach. It's something I had to dig out for myself, question by question and prompt by prompt.
But when you have that environment set up, you can just kind of run and like run fast.

So the data is the unique insight, the data point that the model doesn't have access to yet, the personal experience, all of those things that are working are ultimately going to make the writing unique.
AI is just as powerful as a supportive technology.
So compounding is the idea that every piece of feedback that you give to AI should feed back into the system to improve the next output.

if there's a bomb under the table and it explodes, that's a one moment of surprise. But if you have people sitting around the table and you show the audience the bomb under the table and say this bomb will go off in five minutes, now you have five minutes of suspense.
what I want to challenge the AI community with is thinking about how we can expand those kinds of opportunities to more people and more kinds of people in more different places.
